820.title: Digging in the desert
820.hook: a caravan out of water; a boy hammers through the rock and finds it (Jataka 2)
820.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell this tale to encourage effort, viriya, one of the perfections, especially to people who have grown discouraged in their practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two caravans: one poured out its water on a stranger's word, one checked the sky. Your line was keep the water. Did you hold on to one sensible habit? Today, another caravan, and this one has already run dry. Day eight hundred twenty.

The sand is too hot to cross by day, so the caravan travels at night, steered by a guide who reads the stars. Late in the journey, the guide falls asleep. The oxen wander, turn, and walk all night in a circle. At dawn the merchants look around and see their own campsite from yesterday. They've used up their water and their firewood. That's where the second tale of the Jataka begins: lost, dry, and back at the start.
screen: `TRAVELING BY THE STARS.` → `THE GUIDE FALLS ASLEEP.` → `BACK AT THE START.`

segments.voice: First, the despair. The caravan people lie down under their carts and give up. The leader, the bodhisatta, thinks: if I give up too, everyone dies. So while it's still cool, he walks the camp, looking. Second, the grass. He finds a clump of kusa grass growing in the sand. Grass means water somewhere below, he reasons. He calls for spades and has the men dig. They dig, and dig, deep into the ground, and then the spades hit rock. Nothing. The men drop their tools. They're done. Third, the listening. The bodhisatta climbs down into the pit and lays his ear against the stone. Underneath, faintly, he hears water running. He climbs out and turns to a serving boy. If you give up, he tells him, we're all lost. Go down with the hammer, and strike the rock. Fourth, the boy. The boy goes down when the grown men have quit. He swings the hammer, again and again, and the rock splits. Water rises up the shaft, the tale says, as tall as a palm tree. Everyone drinks. They cook, they rest, and they travel on. The tale's frame story is about a monk who'd given up on his practice, and the Buddha tells him this tale to remind him that in a past life he was the boy with the hammer. The one who kept going. Look at who saves the caravan. Not the leader, not the men with the spades. A serving boy, doing one more swing.
screen: `THEY LIE DOWN AND GIVE UP.` · `GRASS, A PIT, THEN ROCK.` · `AN EAR AGAINST THE STONE.` · `THE BOY SWINGS ONCE MORE.` · then, large: `DIG ONCE MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep going one step more. Bring to mind one thing you've stopped working on because it hit rock. A project, a conversation, a habit. Don't promise to finish it. Just hold it, and listen, the way the bodhisatta listened through the stone. Is there anything running underneath? If there is, choose one small swing you could take today: one email, one page, one try. If there isn't, that's information too. Then breathe and rest. The bell holds the time.
Viriya. Effort, energy: what a boy showed, swinging a hammer until the water came, after a lost caravan's pit hit rock. Today's word.
Your line: dig once more. Today, when you reach the point where you'd usually stop, take one more swing. Just one. Day eight hundred twenty.

options: refuse. if the men couldn't, you can't.

original.note: Pali viriya: effort, energy. it's one of the ten perfections, and this tale is told for it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about not giving up.
what it means: when the men quit at the rock, a boy keeps swinging, and the whole caravan lives.
what a scholar hears: the frame story is about a discouraged monk, and the tale's last line names him as the boy in that past life; it's taught for viriya, effort.

821.title: A dead mouse
821.hook: a young man turns a dead mouse into a fortune by steady small trades (Jataka 4)
821.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the tale of the little treasurer as an encouragement to begin practice with whatever is at hand and keep at it steadily.

segments.voice: Yesterday, digging in the desert: a boy swung the hammer with viriya, effort, once more, and the water came. Your line was dig once more. Did you take one more swing? Today, a fortune that starts with something nobody wants. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

A dead mouse is lying in the street. A wealthy treasurer, on his way to the king, glances down and says out loud: a sharp young man could pick that up and start a business. A passerby might laugh. One young man, poor and standing close enough to hear every word, doesn't laugh. He picks the mouse up. That's the fourth tale of the Jataka, and the treasurer making the remark is the bodhisatta.
screen: `A MOUSE IN THE STREET.` → `A REMARK IN PASSING.` → `ONE MAN PICKS IT UP.`

segments.voice: First, the mouse. The young man sells it at a tavern, as food for the cat, for one tiny copper coin. That's the whole starting capital. Second, the trades. With the coin he buys a bit of molasses and a jar of water. He waits for the flower gatherers coming home hot and tired, gives them a drink and a taste of sweetness, and they give him flowers. He sells the flowers. He does it again. After a storm, he gathers fallen branches from the king's garden and sells the wood to a potter. He gives water to the grass cutters, and later, when horse dealers come to town, those grass cutters sell him their grass. Each step is tiny. None of them is clever on its own. Third, the patience. Bit by bit, by watching what people need and waiting for the moment, the young man becomes rich. Not by luck. By a long line of small, honest trades, each one paying for the next. Fourth, the return. When he's done well, he goes back to the treasurer whose passing remark started it all, and brings him a gift and tells him the story. The treasurer, delighted, gives the young man his daughter in marriage, and in time the young man takes his place as treasurer. The tale is told in the Jataka for a monk who'd been slow and discouraged at the start, and its point is spiritual as much as financial: steady small effort, started with whatever is lying in front of you, adds up. The young man began with a mouse.
screen: `SOLD FOR ONE TINY COIN.` · `WATER, FLOWERS, BRANCHES, GRASS.` · `EACH SMALL TRADE PAYS THE NEXT.` · `BACK TO THE MAN WHO SAID IT.` · then, large: `FROM A DEAD MOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: start small today. Choose something you've wanted to begin and haven't, because you don't have enough yet. Enough time, enough money, enough skill. Now look for the dead mouse: the smallest, plainest piece of it that's already lying in front of you. Five minutes. One question. One page. Name that one piece to yourself, and let it be enough for today. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Starting capital. The dead mouse a poor young man sold for one coin, the whole starting capital that steady small trades turned into a whole new life. Today's word.
Your line: from a dead mouse. Today, start the thing you've been putting off with the smallest piece you already have, and don't wait for more. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

what a scholar hears: the Jataka tells it for a monk who was slow and discouraged at first; the business is a picture of steady effort in practice, and the tale's last line names who each character was.

822.title: The dancing peacock
822.hook: a peacock dances without modesty and loses his bride (Jataka 32)
822.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Nacca Jataka as a lesson in restraint and a sense of shame, hiri and ottappa in Pali.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a young man built a fortune with a dead mouse as his starting capital. Your line was from a dead mouse. Did you start something small? Today, someone who already has everything, and throws it away in a minute. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

Every bird in the mountains has gathered in one place. The king of the birds, a golden goose, has promised his daughter she may choose her own husband, and now she walks along the rows of feathered hopefuls. She stops in front of the peacock, with his jewel-colored neck and his patterned tail, and says: that one. In the Nacca Jataka, that should be the end. It's the beginning of his mistake.
screen: `ALL THE BIRDS GATHER.` → `SHE CHOOSES HER OWN.` → `SHE CHOOSES THE PEACOCK.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. In a time long ago, the tale says, the four-footed animals made the lion their king, the fish chose a great fish, and the birds chose the golden goose. His daughter asks one wish of her father: to pick her husband herself. He agrees, and calls the assembly. Second, the choice. She picks the peacock. The other birds go to him with the news. And he's so thrilled, so eager to show what he's got, that he says: she hasn't even seen my dancing yet. Third, the dance. Right there, in front of the king, the bride, and every bird in the mountains, the peacock spreads his feathers wide and dances. He's so busy showing off that he forgets himself completely and loses every bit of modesty, there in the middle of the crowd. Fourth, the cost. The golden goose is embarrassed for everyone. He speaks a verse: your voice is pleasant, your back is lovely, your neck has the color of a jewel, but for that dance I won't give you my daughter. He has no shame inside and no restraint outside, the king says. And he gives his daughter instead to a young goose, his own nephew. The peacock flies off, ashamed. Notice what the tale doesn't say. It doesn't say the peacock was ugly, or unworthy, or unloved. He'd already been chosen. Nothing more was needed from him. The win was finished, and the urge to prove it is what undid it. The Jataka tells it for a monk who forgot restraint in front of everyone.
screen: `A LION, A FISH, A GOLDEN GOOSE.` · `SHE PICKS THE PEACOCK.` · `HE DANCES IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` · `GIVEN TO THE YOUNG GOOSE INSTEAD.` · then, large: `THE DANCE COST HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: skip one chance to show off. Bring to mind a place where you're tempted to. A meeting, a group chat, a dinner table, a post you're about to share. Notice the little lift in the chest, the urge to make sure everyone sees. Don't scold it. Just feel it rise, and feel it pass, the way a breath rises and passes. Whatever is already settled can stay settled. Rest in that, and let the dance stay undanced. The bell holds the time.
Modesty. What the peacock lost, dancing to show off after he was already chosen, and so lost the bride he'd already won. Today's word.
Your line: the dance cost him. Today, when you feel the urge to prove what's already settled, keep your feathers folded once. Day eight hundred twenty-two.

823.title: Who is eldest
823.hook: a partridge, a monkey and an elephant decide by the banyan tree who should be honored (Jataka 37)
823.howItsDone: In Buddhist monastic communities, monks and nuns are seated and greeted in order of seniority since ordination, and lay Buddhists may greet elders with a bow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dancing peacock lost his modesty, showed off, and lost the bride he'd already won. Your line was the dance cost him. Did you keep your feathers folded? Today, three friends who need to sort out who goes first. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

A partridge, a monkey and an elephant share a home under a great banyan tree. They're friends, more or less. But they keep stepping on each other: nobody listens, nobody defers, nobody knows whose word should count. So one day they agree on a fix. Whoever is oldest gets the honor, and the others will listen to him. Simple. Except none of them knows who that is. The Tittira Jataka is how they find out.
screen: `THREE FRIENDS, ONE TREE.` → `NOBODY DEFERS.` → `BUT WHO IS OLDEST?`

segments.voice: First, the elephant. When I was young, he says, this banyan was just a little bush. I used to walk right over it, and its top branches brushed my belly. So I remember this tree when it was tiny. Second, the monkey. When I was young, he says, I'd sit on the ground and nibble the topmost shoots of this banyan without even stretching my neck. So I remember it even smaller than that. Third, the partridge. There used to be another great banyan, he says, over in another place. I ate one of its fruits, and I dropped the seed right here. This tree grew from that. So I knew this tree before it was a tree at all. The other two agree at once: the partridge is the eldest. From then on they honor him, listen to his advice, and the tale says they lived well together. Fourth, the frame. In the present-day story, the Buddha hears that his senior disciple Sariputta spent a night outside, because younger monks had taken every place to sleep. He tells this tale, and teaches that in the community, places and respect go by seniority in the order, not by birth or status. Three animals worked it out by asking a simple question. Notice that each one's claim is a memory, and the oldest memory wins. Honor here isn't flattery. It's a way of making room, so a crowded home under one tree can get along.
screen: `THE ELEPHANT: A BUSH I WALKED OVER.` · `THE MONKEY: I ATE ITS TOP SHOOTS.` · `THE PARTRIDGE: I DROPPED THE SEED.` · `SARIPUTTA SLEPT OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `HONOR THE ELDEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one elder. Bring to mind someone who was there before you. A grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor, a colleague who's been around longer than you have. Someone who remembers the tree as a seed. Hold their face for a few breaths. Then think of one small way to give them a place today: ask their advice, let them speak first, or simply tell them you remember something they taught you. Choose it, and rest. The bell holds the time.
Seniority. What a partridge, a monkey and an elephant settle by the oldest memory of their tree, and the partridge wins. Today's word.
Your line: honor the eldest. Today, let one person who came before you go first, or ask them what they remember. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 823 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CRANE AND THE CRAB.`

824.title: The crane and the crab
824.hook: a crane promises fish a better lake and eats them, until the crab (Jataka 38)
824.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the tale of the crane and the crab as a warning that deceit can turn back on the deceiver.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a partridge, a monkey and an elephant settled seniority by the partridge's memory, and the partridge won. Your line was honor the eldest. Did someone who came before you go first? Today, a promise that sounds wonderful. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

It's the hot season, and the pond is shrinking. The fish can feel the walls of mud closing in. And on the bank, a crane stands very still, looking sad on their behalf. When they ask what's wrong, he says he's been worrying about them. He knows a big lake not far off, deep, cool, full of lotuses. He'd be glad to carry them there, one at a time. Free of charge. In the Baka Jataka, the fish have an answer ready.
screen: `A POND DRYING UP.` → `A SAD-LOOKING CRANE.` → `A BETTER LAKE, FREE.`

segments.voice: First, the doubt. The fish aren't fools. They tell the crane plainly: we've never heard of a crane who cared about fish. You want to eat us. So the crane offers proof. Send one of you with me to see the lake, he says. They pick a big fish, blind in one eye, and the crane really does carry him to the lake, lets him swim around, and brings him back. The old fish tells everyone: it's real. Second, the trap. Now the fish line up. One at a time, the crane carries each one off, but not to the lake. He flies to a tree beside it, pins the fish in a fork of the branches, and eats it. Then he goes back for the next. The pile of bones under the tree grows. Third, the crab. At last the pond is empty of fish. Only a crab is left. The crane offers him the same trip. The crab says yes, but I'd better hold on to your neck with my claws so I don't fall. On the way, the crab sees the tree and the bones underneath. And the crane says it out loud: I'm going to eat you too. Fourth, the grip. The crab squeezes. Take me to the water, he says, or I'll take your head. The crane, choking, sets him down at the edge of the lake. And the crab snips through his neck anyway. A tree spirit who watched it all, the bodhisatta in this tale, speaks a verse: guile doesn't profit the guileful; look what the crane got from the crab. The crab never trusted the offer. He held on.
screen: `ONE FISH SENT TO CHECK.` · `A TREE, A PILE OF BONES.` · `THE CRAB HOLDS THE NECK.` · `THE TRICKSTER MEETS THE CRAB.` · then, large: `THE CRAB REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one promise that's too good. Pick one offer in your life right now that sounds wonderful. A deal, a message, an app, a person saying they'll take care of everything. Ask the fishes' first question: does this kind of helper usually care about me? Then the crab's question: where's my grip, if it turns out to be wrong? You don't need to decide anything. Just hold both questions gently, and breathe with them. The bell holds the time.
Baka. Crane or heron: the bird whose sweet offer ate every fish, until a crab kept hold of its neck. Today's word.
Your line: the crab remembers. Today, when an offer sounds too good, keep one claw on it until you've seen the tree. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

original.note: Pali baka: crane or heron. the tale's name, Baka Jataka, comes from it.

825.title: The monkey gardeners
825.hook: monkeys water the saplings by pulling each one up to check its roots (Jataka 46)
825.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Aramadusaka Jataka as a lesson that good intentions need wisdom too, and that checking too soon can do harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the baka, the crane, and the crab: a sweet promise, a pile of bones, and a crab who held on. Your line was the crab remembers. Did you keep a claw on one offer? Today, helpers who mean well, and ruin everything. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

There's a festival in the city of Benares, crowds and celebration in every street, and the king's gardener badly wants to go. But the young trees in the royal park need water while he's away. Then he has an idea. A troop of monkeys lives in the park. They eat the fruit, they enjoy the shade; surely they owe him a favor. He goes to their king and asks. The monkey king says: of course. Leave it to us.
screen: `A FESTIVAL IN THE CITY.` → `THE SAPLINGS NEED WATER.` → `LEAVE IT TO US.`

segments.voice: First, the job. The gardener hands over the water skins and the wooden pots and goes off to the festival. The monkey king gathers his troop and gives the order to water the young trees. Second, the plan. But water is precious, the monkey king tells them. We mustn't waste it. So before you water a tree, pull it up and look at its roots. Trees with long roots get a lot. Trees with short roots get a little. It's careful. It's thrifty. It sounds like good management. Third, the result. So the monkeys go through the park, tree by tree, pulling each sapling out of the ground, inspecting the roots, and watering accordingly. And every young tree they check, they kill. Fourth, the witness. A wise man walking through the park, the bodhisatta in this tale, sees the monkeys at work and asks what they're doing. They explain: their king's orders. And he says, in a verse, that the ignorant, trying to do good, do harm instead, like the monkeys in the king's garden. What makes the tale sharp is that nobody is wicked. The monkeys aren't lazy, and they aren't greedy. They're conscientious. They wanted to be sure. And being sure, here, meant digging up the very thing that needed to stay hidden in the dark to grow. A root does its work out of sight.
screen: `THE GARDENER GOES TO THE FESTIVAL.` · `CHECK THE ROOTS, SAVE THE WATER.` · `EVERY TREE THEY CHECK DIES.` · `HARM FROM TRYING TO HELP.` · then, large: `DON'T PULL UP THE ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing grow unchecked. Bring to mind something young in your life. A plan, a relationship, a habit, a skill, someone you're helping along. Notice if you've been pulling it up to look at its roots. Checking it, measuring it, asking if it's working yet. Now picture setting it back in the ground and patting the soil down. Water it, and leave it alone. Breathe, and let it be underground for a while. The bell holds the time.
Conscientious. What the monkey gardeners were, careful helpers who pulled up every sapling to measure its roots, and killed what they meant to save. Today's word.
Your line: don't pull up the roots. Today, catch yourself once checking on something that needs time, and leave it in the ground instead. Day eight hundred twenty-five.

826.title: The virtuous elephant
826.hook: an elephant rescues a lost man, who comes back to saw off his tusks (Jataka 72)
826.tomorrow: The fish who prayed for rain
826.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the Silavanaga Jataka as a picture of generosity and patience that don't depend on gratitude, and as a warning about where ingratitude leads.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the monkey gardeners, so conscientious, pulled up every sapling to check it. Your line was don't pull up the roots. Did you leave one thing in the ground? Today, kindness that keeps going after it's been betrayed. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

A man from Benares has gone into the forest for work and lost his way. He wanders, crying out in fear. Then a huge white elephant steps out of the trees. The man runs. The elephant stops. The man stops. The elephant steps forward; the man runs again. Finally the man understands: this animal means no harm. He's the bodhisatta, the tale says, and he's come to help. Today's story is what the man does with that help.
screen: `A MAN LOST IN THE FOREST.` → `A WHITE ELEPHANT APPEARS.` → `HE COMES TO HELP.`

segments.voice: First, the rescue. The elephant takes the man to his home, feeds him on fruit, and then carries him on his back out of the forest to the road. But as they go, the man quietly takes note of every tree and every hill along the way. Second, the bargain. Back in Benares, he walks down the street of the ivory carvers and asks: what would you pay for the tusks of a living elephant? A lot, they say. So he takes a saw and goes back. Third, the gift. He finds the elephant and says he's poor and has nothing to live on. Would the elephant give him his tusks? The elephant kneels down and lets him saw. He gives them freely, and says it isn't that he doesn't value them: the wisdom he is seeking is dearer to him than these. The man sells them. Then he comes back for what's left. The elephant gives that too. Then he comes back a third time, and digs out the roots of the tusks from the elephant's face. Each time, the elephant lets him. Fourth, the end. As the man walks away, the tale says, the earth splits open under him and swallows him. A tree spirit who saw it all speaks a verse: give an ungrateful man the whole world, and it still won't satisfy him. Notice where the tale's weight falls. It never calls the elephant foolish. He gives three times, each gift costing more, and the tale saves its judgment for the taker. The man's ingratitude doesn't get to decide who the elephant is. The tale's last line names the man as Devadatta, whose ingratitude toward the Buddha is the frame of the story.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one ingratitude. Bring to mind a time someone took your help and gave nothing back, or worse. Not the deepest wound you carry; a small one. Notice whatever comes up with it. You don't have to approve of what they did; forgiving isn't approving. Just see if you can set the weight of it down for a moment, the way he knelt. Breathe out. Let your kindness belong to you, not to them. The bell holds the time.
Sila. Virtue, good conduct: what the virtuous elephant showed, rescuing a lost man, then giving him tusks, stumps and roots, and staying good to the end. Today's word.

Your line: good to the ungrateful. This week: dig once more, from a dead mouse, the dance cost him, honor the eldest, the crab remembers, don't pull up the roots. Today, do one kindness and expect no thanks. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

myth: the tale calls the elephant a fool for giving
it never does; it saves its judgment for the man who kept taking.
the man came back three times
first for the tusks, then for the stumps, then for the roots.
the tale names the man in a past life of Devadatta
its last line identifies him as Devadatta.

fork.setup: you're the elephant. the man you carried out of the forest is back with a saw, asking for your tusks. what do you do?
options: drive him off. you saved his life once already.
kneel and let him take them.
give him fruit instead and send him home.
fork.reveal: the elephant kneels and lets him saw, saying the wisdom he seeks is dearer to him than tusks, and gives again each time he returns.

original.note: Pali sila: virtue, good conduct. the tale's name, Silavanaga, means the virtuous elephant.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad story about a greedy man.
what it means: the elephant stays generous even while he's being used, and the ungrateful man is never satisfied.

what a scholar hears: the tale's last line names the man as Devadatta, so it's told in the frame of Devadatta's ingratitude toward the Buddha; the elephant practices the perfections of generosity and patience.
